entries.title: Vegetarian-fed, omega-3, soy-free
entries.question: What do the feed claims on an egg carton mean?
entries.decision: ‘Vegetarian-fed’ is the one to walk away from.
entries.why: Hens are omnivores. That claim and a real pasture claim work against each other.
entries.short_answer: ‘Vegetarian-fed’ reads as an upgrade and quietly works against a genuine pasture claim, because a hen with real outdoor access is eating insects and worms. The rest of the feed words are plainer. ‘Soy-free’ and ‘corn-free’ mean exactly what they say and have to be printed. ‘Omega-3 enriched’ means flax or algae in the ration, and the egg really does carry more, though the amount is not standardized.
entries.detail: The space claims (cage-free, free-range, pasture-raised) never touch feed, so the feed words carry that job alone. ‘Vegetarian-fed’ reads as an upgrade and quietly works against a genuine pasture claim, because a hen with real outdoor access eats insects and worms. Omega-3 enrichment is real chemistry rather than marketing, but with no set quantity two enriched cartons can differ a lot. Certified organic reaches feed and requires it be organic, which in practice is usually organic soy and organic corn. Organic answers how the feed was grown, not what the feed is.
sources: USDA FSIS labeling policy on feed claims
USDA National Organic Program, 7 CFR 205.237 (livestock feed requirements)
Poultry-science literature on omega-3 enrichment of eggs
entries.kristy_take: A hen on real pasture is eating bugs. That claim says she was not.
buying_tips: Space claims and feed claims are separate words. One never implies the other.
‘Soy-free’ and ‘corn-free’ have to be printed. Nothing else on the carton implies them.
‘Omega-3 enriched’ means flax or algae in the ration. The amount is not standardized.
‘Vegetarian-fed’ means no animal protein in the feed, which sits oddly beside a real pasture claim.
Organic requires organic feed, usually organic soy and corn. Not a different kind of feed.

entries.title: Why US eggs live in the fridge
entries.question: Do eggs have to be refrigerated?
entries.decision: Washed eggs live cold, in the carton, on a middle shelf.
entries.why: Washing strips the cuticle that seals a porous shell. Unwashed farm eggs keep theirs.
entries.short_answer: In the US, yes. Eggs sold here are washed at the plant, and washing strips the cuticle, the natural coating that seals a porous shell. Once it is gone the egg needs constant refrigeration. Unwashed farm eggs keep their cuticle and can sit out, which is why cartons sit on an open shelf across much of Europe. What you should not do is move an egg between the two.
entries.detail: US rules require washing and sanitizing, then holding at 45F or below from the plant onward. Neither system is wrong; they solve the same problem from opposite ends. In the carton on a middle shelf is the right spot, not the door, where the temperature swings every time it opens. A cold egg brought to room temperature sweats, and moisture on a porous shell is exactly what the cuticle was preventing. Farm eggs bought unwashed can live on the counter, but the moment you wash them they join the fridge rules.
sources: USDA FSIS shell egg refrigeration requirements (45F)
FDA Egg Safety Final Rule
EU marketing standards for eggs (unwashed, ambient storage)
entries.kristy_take: Washed eggs lost their seal, so they live cold. Unwashed farm eggs kept theirs, so they do not. Just do not switch an egg between the two.
buying_tips: Store the carton on a middle shelf, not the door. The door swings warm every time it opens.
Keep them in the carton. It slows moisture loss and keeps odors out.
Unwashed farm eggs can stay on the counter. Once washed, they need the fridge for good.
Leftover raw whites and yolks keep a few days covered. Yolks want a little water over them.

entries.title: USDA beef grades: Prime, Choice, Select
entries.question: What do Prime, Choice and Select mean?
entries.decision: Pay for grade on a quick-cooked steak. Skip it on anything braised.
entries.why: Grade measures marbling and age. It says nothing about how the animal was raised.
entries.short_answer: They grade marbling, the fat threaded inside the muscle, along with the age of the animal. Prime has the most, Choice is the middle and the usual retail grade, Select is leanest and driest. It is a cooking and eating-quality scale. It says nothing about how the animal was raised, what it was fed, or whether it ever got outside.
entries.detail: Grading is voluntary and paid for by the packer, so plenty of good beef carries no grade at all, including much grass-finished beef, whose marbling pattern the scale was not built around. Marbling melts during cooking, which is why a Prime steak forgives high heat and a Select one dries out. On a braising cut the grade matters far less, because time and moisture do the work the fat would have done. Grade and sourcing are two separate axes, and neither implies the other.
sources: USDA AMS Official United States Standards for Grades of Carcass Beef
USDA AMS voluntary beef grading program
entries.kristy_take: Grade measures fat inside the muscle and nothing else. A Select chuck roast cooked low and slow beats a Prime steak cooked badly.
buying_tips: Prime, Choice, Select is a marbling scale, top to bottom.
Grading is voluntary. Ungraded is not a downgrade, and a lot of grass-finished beef skips it.
Pay up for grade on a quick-cooked steak. Skip it on anything braised.
Grade and sourcing are separate questions. Neither answers the other.

entries.title: Judging meat at the case
aliases: how to tell if meat is fresh
entries.question: How do I tell good meat from the case?
entries.decision: Press it, look at the tray, smell it. Ignore the color.
entries.why: Color is oxygen. Firm springy flesh and a dry tray are what actually tell you.
entries.short_answer: Color is the least useful signal and the one everybody uses. Bright red is beef that has met oxygen, purple-red is vacuum-packed beef that has not, and both are fine. Dull brown at the edges means it has been cut a while. What actually tells you: firm springy flesh, fine marbling through the muscle rather than a rim of fat, a dry tray, and no sour smell.
entries.detail: Beef pigment turns bright red within minutes of oxygen exposure and oxidizes browner over days. That is surface chemistry, not spoilage, which is why a vacuum-sealed roast looks purple and a freshly cut steak looks cherry-red. The liquid pooled in a tray, called purge, is the useful tell: a lot of it means the meat has sat, or was frozen and thawed, and it carries flavor away with it. Marbling should run through the muscle in fine threads; a thick outer fat cap is trim, not marbling. Sell-by dates are set by the store. Trust your nose over any of them.
sources: USDA FSIS “The Color of Meat and Poultry”
USDA FSIS meat labeling and product dating guidance
entries.kristy_take: Color is oxygen, not quality. Press it, look at the tray, smell it. Those three beat the sticker.
buying_tips: Firm and springy, not soft or tacky. It should push back.
Fine marbling through the muscle beats a thick fat cap on the outside.
A dry tray is a good sign. Pooled liquid means it has sat, or was frozen and thawed.
Purple beef is vacuum-packed, not spoiled. Brown edges mean older, not unsafe.
Take it from the back of the case where it is coldest, and get it home cold.

entries.title: What to ask the butcher
entries.question: What should I ask at the butcher counter?
entries.decision: Ask what came in today and what is coming down in price.
entries.why: The counter is free expertise. Custom grinds, portioning and bones are usually included.
entries.short_answer: The service counter is free expertise most shoppers walk straight past. Ask what came in today, ask the sourcing question directly, and ask for a custom grind or a cut portioned the way you want it. Ask for bones and trim, which are often cheap or free and make stock. Ask what is coming down in price this week, then build the week around the answer.
entries.detail: A staffed counter answers things a package never will: whether the beef is grass-finished, whether the chicken was air-chilled, when it was actually cut. They will grind a chuck roast fresh, which beats the pre-packed tray and lets you choose the cut. They will french a rack, tie a roast, portion a whole fish. At most counters none of that costs extra. The cheap cuts sit in the same case, and the person behind the glass usually knows exactly how to cook them.
sources: USDA Institutional Meat Purchase Specifications (cut nomenclature)
entries.kristy_take: The counter is free expertise. Ask what came in today and what is cheap this week, then build dinner from the answer.
buying_tips: Ask what came in today, and what is coming down in price.
Ask for a custom grind. A chuck roast ground fresh beats the pre-packed tray.
Ask for bones and trim. Often cheap or free, and they make stock.
Ask the sourcing question outright: grass-finished, air-chilled, where from.
Ask them to portion it. Cutting, tying and boning are usually included.
entries.tier_note: Using the counter is a shopping habit offered as a standard, not a claim about the meat.

entries.title: Chicken cuts: breast, thigh, whole bird
entries.question: Which cut of chicken should I buy?
entries.decision: Bone-in thighs. Boneless skinless is the priciest form of the same bird.
entries.why: Dark meat is forgiving and hard to overcook. Boneless skinless is the priciest form of it.
entries.short_answer: Whole bird is the cheapest per pound and leaves a carcass for stock. Thighs are dark meat: more fat, more flavor, and very hard to overcook. Breast is lean and fast and goes dry the moment you look away. Bone-in and skin-on cost less and cook better than boneless skinless, which is the most expensive way to buy the same bird.
entries.detail: Dark meat comes from muscles the bird actually used, so it carries more fat and stays juicy across a wide window of doneness. Breast is a low-use muscle: lean, quick, unforgiving. Bones conduct heat slowly and skin renders and bastes, which is why bone-in skin-on thighs are the most forgiving thing in the case. Boneless skinless breast is convenience paid for twice, once at the register and again in how fast it dries. A whole bird broken down at home gives you both kinds of meat plus a frame for broth, at the lowest cost per pound in the store.
sources: USDA FoodData Central (poultry composition)
USDA FSIS poultry labeling terms
entries.kristy_take: Bone-in thighs are the most forgiving protein in the store. A whole bird is the cheapest, and the frame makes stock.
buying_tips: Whole bird: cheapest per pound, and the carcass makes stock.
Thighs, bone-in and skin-on: forgiving, cheap, hard to overcook.
Breast: fast and lean. Pull it the moment it is done.
Boneless skinless is the priciest form of the same bird.
Check the label for ‘retained water’, and for ‘air-chilled’ if skin matters to you.

labels_decoded.meaning: Working muscle. More fat, more flavor, a wide margin for error.

entries.title: Pork cuts and ‘solution added’ pork
entries.question: Which pork cut should I buy, and what does ‘solution added’ mean?
entries.decision: Pork shoulder. And read the label for ‘solution added’.
entries.why: Shoulder is the value cut in the case. ‘Enhanced’ means injected brine, sold by the pound.
entries.short_answer: Same rule as beef: hard-working muscles go low and slow, lean ones go fast. Shoulder (Boston butt, picnic) is the braising and pulled-pork cut and it is cheap. Loin and tenderloin are lean and quick. The label to find is ‘enhanced’ or ‘contains up to X% solution’, which means injected saltwater and phosphates. You buy that liquid by the pound, and it is already salted.
entries.detail: A large share of retail pork is pumped with a solution of water, salt and phosphates to hold moisture, because modern pork is bred lean and dries out. The percentage has to be declared. It is not unsafe, and it does make a lean chop more forgiving, but it changes what you paid for and it pre-seasons the meat, so a second brine oversalts it. Unenhanced pork browns better and tastes more like pork. Shoulder is the value cut of the whole animal: fatty, forgiving, and it feeds a crowd for very little.
sources: USDA FSIS labeling requirements for enhanced and solution-added meat
USDA Institutional Meat Purchase Specifications (pork cut nomenclature)

buying_tips: Braise or pull: shoulder, Boston butt, picnic, country-style ribs.
Fast and lean: loin chops, tenderloin. Pull them early.

entries.title: ‘Uncured’ deli meat
entries.question: Is ‘uncured’ deli meat actually nitrite-free?
entries.decision: ‘Uncured’ is cured with celery powder. Find the asterisk.
entries.why: Celery juice powder is a concentrated natural nitrate source. Same chemistry, different source.
entries.short_answer: No, and the package says so if you find the asterisk. ‘Uncured, no nitrates or nitrites added’ is required to be followed by a qualifier along the lines of ‘except those naturally occurring in celery powder’. Celery juice powder is a concentrated natural nitrate source, so the meat is cured, just with a vegetable-derived agent rather than a synthetic one.
entries.detail: USDA labeling rules force that qualifier, which is why every ‘uncured’ package carries a footnote most shoppers never read. The chemistry that fixes the color and preserves the meat is the same either way; only the source of the nitrate differs, and measured residual levels are broadly comparable. That does not make it a scam, it makes it a sourcing preference, and it is worth knowing that ‘uncured’ is a different statement from ‘no nitrites’. The bigger question at the deli case is how much processed meat a week holds, not which curing agent was used.
sources: USDA FSIS labeling policy on ‘uncured’ and ‘no nitrate or nitrite added’ claims
Peer-reviewed comparisons of residual nitrite in conventionally and naturally cured meats
entries.kristy_take: ‘Uncured’ means cured with celery powder. The asterisk on the package says so. Same chemistry, different source.
buying_tips: Find the asterisk. ‘Uncured’ is always qualified on the label.

Sliced at the counter is usually a shorter ingredient list than the pre-packed tub.

entries.title: Mercury by fish
aliases: which fish are low in mercury
entries.question: Which fish are low in mercury and which are high?
entries.decision: Small and short-lived. Sardines, salmon, skipjack.
entries.why: Mercury tracks size and lifespan. The big long-lived predators carry the most.
entries.short_answer: It tracks size and lifespan almost perfectly. Small, short-lived fish carry the least and the big long-lived predators carry the most. Sardines, salmon and canned light (skipjack) tuna sit at the bottom; swordfish, shark, king mackerel and bigeye tuna sit at the top. FDA and EPA publish it as a three-tier list and aim the advice at pregnant and nursing women and young children.
entries.detail: Methylmercury accumulates up the food chain, so a fish that ate thousands of smaller fish across twenty years carries far more than one that lived two years on plankton. That is why the pattern is so predictable by species. FDA and EPA publish it as a three-tier list (Best Choices, Good Choices, Choices to Avoid) and direct the advice at pregnant and nursing women and young children. This is information about the fish. Anything about a personal medical situation belongs with a doctor.
sources: FDA/EPA ‘Advice About Eating Fish’ (2021 update)
FDA mercury concentrations in commercial fish and shellfish
entries.kristy_take: Small and short-lived is the entire rule. Sardines, salmon and skipjack sit at the bottom of the chain, and they are the cheap ones.
buying_tips: Lowest: sardines, anchovies, salmon, shrimp, scallops, tilapia, cod, pollock, catfish, canned light tuna.
Middle: albacore and yellowfin tuna, halibut, grouper, snapper, mahi mahi.
Highest: swordfish, shark, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, bigeye tuna, Gulf tilefish.

entries.title: Telling fresh at the fish counter
aliases: how to tell fish is fresh
entries.question: How do I tell if fish at the counter is fresh?
entries.decision: Smell it first. Clean seawater or nothing means yes.
entries.why: Sharp or ammonia means it has gone. Then check the eyes, the gills and the ice.
entries.short_answer: Smell first. Fresh fish smells like clean seawater or like almost nothing. A sharp fishy or ammonia note means it has gone. Then look: on a whole fish, clear domed eyes, bright red gills, tight scales, flesh that springs back. On fillets, a translucent sheen, flakes still holding together, no browning at the edges, and no liquid pooled underneath.
entries.detail: The ‘fishy’ smell people associate with fish is the smell of it breaking down, which makes it the single best gauge in the case. Whole fish tell you more than fillets, because eyes, gills and skin all age visibly. On a fillet the tell is gaping: muscle segments separate as it ages and the flesh loses its sheen. Ice matters as much as the fish, so it should be sitting on plenty of it and not in a puddle. Asking them to hand you a piece to smell is completely normal, and any good counter will.
sources: FDA Fish and Fishery Products Hazards and Controls Guidance (sensory evaluation)
NOAA Fisheries seafood handling guidance
entries.kristy_take: Ask to smell it. Clean seawater or nothing means yes. Sharp and fishy means put it back.
buying_tips: Smell it. Clean and briny is right. Sharp, fishy or ammonia is not.
Whole fish: clear domed eyes, bright red gills, tight scales, flesh that springs back.
Fillets: a translucent sheen, flakes holding together, no browning at the edge.
It should sit on plenty of ice, not in a pool of its own liquid.
Ask when it came in and whether it was previously frozen. Both are fair questions.

labels_decoded.meaning: Flakes separating on a fillet. A sign it has aged.

entries.tier_note: The smell of spoilage is a documented chemical change, not an opinion about the fish.

entries.title: Buying canned fish
entries.question: What should I look for in canned fish?
entries.decision: Packed in olive oil or water. Bones and skin left in.
entries.why: The list should read fish, oil or water, salt. Anything longer is a sauce.
entries.short_answer: Read what it is packed in. Olive oil or water are the clean options; plenty of tins use soybean, cottonseed or unnamed ‘vegetable oil’, which matters if seed oils are a line you hold. Buy sardines and salmon with the bones and skin left in. And the ingredient list should read fish, oil or water, and salt. Anything longer is a sauce.
entries.detail: Canned fish is one of the best value whole foods in the store, and the differences between tins are almost entirely the pack medium and what else went in. Oil-packed carries more flavor and, in good olive oil, is worth using in the dish rather than pouring away. Water-packed is leaner and neutral. ‘Vegetable oil’ on a tin is nearly always a seed oil blend and the label will not name which. Skin-on, bone-in sardines and salmon keep the whole small fish intact, which is much of why the tin is worth buying. Flavored tins in sauces bring added sugar and a long list, so read those like any packaged food.
sources: USDA FoodData Central (canned fish composition)
Product ingredient labeling
entries.kristy_take: Packed in olive oil or water. Bones and skin left in. Three ingredients on the back. That is the whole checklist.
buying_tips: Read the pack medium: olive oil or water, not ‘vegetable oil’.
Bone-in and skin-on sardines and salmon. The bones soften completely.
The list should read fish, oil or water, salt. Anything longer is a sauce.
Good oil-packed tins are worth using in the dish rather than draining.
Skipjack (‘light’) sits lower on the mercury range than albacore (‘white’).

entries.title: Which farmed fish are worth buying
entries.question: Is farmed fish worth buying?
entries.decision: Farmed shellfish, trout and char are the good ones.
entries.why: ‘Farmed’ is not a verdict. Mussels and oysters feed themselves by filtering water.
entries.short_answer: It depends entirely on the species and the operation, never on the word ‘farmed’. Farmed shellfish (mussels, oysters, clams) are the standout: they feed themselves by filtering water and need no feed at all. Farmed trout, arctic char and barramundi are generally well regarded. Salmon and shrimp vary enormously by producer and country, which is where certification and origin do real work.
entries.detail: Aquaculture is not one thing. A rope of mussels hanging in a bay takes nothing and adds nothing. A closed recirculating tank system for trout or char is tightly controlled. An open net pen or a coastal shrimp pond depends on the standards of the country and the company running it. So the useful question at the counter is which species and where from, rather than farmed or wild. Wild is the whole-food-standard preference where it is affordable, and that is a preference, not a health verdict on farmed fish. Eating the fish beats skipping it.
sources: NOAA Fisheries aquaculture overviews
Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch species ratings
entries.kristy_take: Farmed shellfish feed themselves by filtering water. That is about as clean as farming protein gets.
buying_tips: Mussels, oysters and clams are farmed almost everywhere and need no feed.
Farmed trout, arctic char and barramundi are generally well regarded.
For salmon and shrimp, ask the country and look for a credible certification.
Country-of-origin is required on unprocessed seafood. Read it.
‘Farmed’ alone is not a verdict. The species and the operation are the question.

entries.title: Seafood seals: MSC, ASC, BAP
entries.question: Do the sustainability seals on seafood mean anything?
entries.decision: MSC on wild. A farm seal is a floor, not a recommendation.
entries.why: Each seal answers one narrow question, and none of them speaks to freshness.
entries.short_answer: The blue MSC label covers wild fisheries and how the stock is managed, which is the one that lines up with buying wild in the first place. ASC and BAP audit farms: published standards, real auditors, and a floor rather than a recommendation. BAP’s one-to-four stars count how far up the chain the audit reached. Seafood Watch is not a label at all, it is a ratings guide you look up.
entries.detail: Each seal answers one question. MSC audits whether a wild fishery is managed so the stock holds and the gear does not wreck the habitat. ASC and BAP audit farms. BAP’s stars count the audited links: one is the processing plant, four adds the farm, hatchery and feed mill. All three publish their standards and send auditors, which is more than an unbacked word on a package offers. What none of them tell you is anything about the fish in front of you: how fresh it is, how it tastes, or how it was handled since.
sources: Marine Stewardship Council fisheries standard
Aquaculture Stewardship Council farm standards
Global Seafood Alliance Best Aquaculture Practices star system
Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch methodology

buying_tips: Blue MSC label: a wild fishery, audited for stock and habitat impact.
ASC: a farm, audited on environmental and social standards.
BAP one to four stars: how many links were audited, from plant up to feed mill.
Seafood Watch is a guide to look up, not a seal to spot.
No seal speaks to freshness. That is still your nose and your eyes.

entries.title: How to pick it, item by item
entries.question: How do I tell if this particular fruit or vegetable is any good?
entries.decision: Pick up two and take the heavier one.
entries.why: Weight means water content, not pith. One habit that beats every color rule going.
entries.short_answer: Every item has one or two checks that actually work, and they are almost never color. Heavy for its size is the near-universal one, because weight means water content rather than pith. Smell at the stem end for anything that ripens off the plant. And turn the berry container over, because that is where the mold starts.
entries.detail: Fruit that keeps ripening after picking (melon, peach, avocado, banana, mango, pear) gives you smell and give as signals. Fruit that does not ripen further once picked (berries, citrus, grapes, pineapple, cherries) has to be bought ready, so those checks are about weight and damage instead. Vegetables are mostly a firmness question: a limp stalk or a rubbery skin means it has been out of the ground a while and lost water. The single best habit is picking up two of the same thing and comparing them by weight. The heavier one is almost always better.
sources: University extension produce selection and ripening guidance
USDA produce grading and handling standards
entries.kristy_take: Pick up two and take the heavier one. That one habit beats every color rule going.
buying_tips: Cantaloupe: creamy gold under the netting, a sweet smell at the stem end, slight give.
Watermelon: a deep yellow field spot, heavy for its size, a hollow thunk.
Pineapple: sweet at the base, deep green leaves, a slight give in the shell. Color is not the tell.
Tomatoes: fragrant at the stem, heavy for their size, and never from the cold case.
Stone fruit: fragrant, with a slight give at the shoulder rather than the tip.
Citrus: heavy for its size, with thin smooth skin. Weight beats color.
Asparagus: tight closed tips and a cut end that is not dried and split.
Broccoli and cauliflower: tight dense heads, no yellowing between the florets.
Leafy greens: perky rather than limp, with no slimy dark patches at the stem base.
Avocado: pop the stem nub — green under it means ripe, brown means overripe, and stuck fast means give it days.
Press with your palm, never your fingertips — fingertip pressure is what bruises the bin.
Buy at staggered firmness so they ripen across the week rather than all on Tuesday.
entries.tier_note: Weight tracking water content is physical, and it is why the heavier of two is the better one.

entries.title: Picking berries
entries.question: How do I pick a good carton of berries?
entries.decision: The carton’s underside decides, not the berries on top.
entries.why: Berries mold from the bottom up under their own weight, long before the top layer shows it.
entries.short_answer: Turn the container over before anything else. The fruit at the bottom carries the load, so it bruises and molds first while the top layer stays presentable long after the carton has turned. A dry, clean underside means it was packed recently and has not sat wet. Juice pooling or a fuzzy spot means decay is already running, and one furry berry takes the punnet.
entries.detail: Berries do not ripen after picking. Unlike a peach or a cantaloupe, what is in the carton is exactly what you are buying — there is no counter-ripening to rescue an underripe punnet, and no reason to buy firm and wait. That makes the carton itself the whole decision. Weight and moisture are what work against it: the bottom layer carries the load, condensation inside a clamshell keeps that layer damp, and mold spreads berry to berry by contact. Clamshells also get re-stacked at the store, so a fresh-looking top layer can sit on fruit that arrived days earlier. Buy them cold, keep them dry, and wash them at the moment you eat them rather than when you unpack.
sources: postharvest handling references for soft fruit (non-climacteric ripening, decay by contact)
USDA produce grading and handling standards
entries.kristy_take: Flip the carton. The top layer is the display and the bottom layer is the truth.
buying_tips: A dry, unstained bottom on the carton. That is the whole check.
No fuzzy white or gray spot on any berry. One takes the punnet.
Green caps still fresh on strawberries, not browned and dry.
Deep, even color for the variety, and uniform size in the container.
Buy them cold, from the refrigerated display rather than a room-temperature stack.
watch_out: Berries do not ripen after picking. Buying firm and waiting does not work the way it does for stone fruit.
Condensation fogging the plastic traps moisture and speeds the mold.

A carton that already smells sweet or fermented is past it.
entries.tier_note: That berries decay from the bottom under their own weight, and do not ripen after picking, is settled postharvest handling — and it is why the underside is the check.

entries.title: Making produce last the week
entries.question: How do I keep produce from going off before I use it?
entries.decision: Wash it when you eat it, not when you unpack it.
entries.why: Moisture is what rots a drawer. Keep the ripening-gas fruit away from greens and berries.
entries.short_answer: Three rules cover most of it. Keep the ethylene producers away from the ethylene sensitive: apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes and stone fruit give off the ripening gas, and greens, broccoli, cucumbers and berries wilt fast beside it. Do not wash anything until you use it. And learn the short list that should never go in the fridge: tomatoes, potatoes, onions, garlic, whole melon and unripe stone fruit.
entries.detail: Ethylene is a plant hormone that triggers ripening and it works on neighbors, which is why a bowl of apples ages the lettuce next to it. Moisture is the other half: water sitting on a leaf or a berry is where mold starts, so the rinse belongs at the moment of eating rather than at unpacking. Cold wrecks texture and flavor in a few specific things. Tomatoes go mealy below about 55F, potatoes convert starch to sugar and brown oddly when cooked, and onions and garlic soften and sprout. Herbs and asparagus keep best standing in a little water like cut flowers, and greens keep best dry with a towel in the bag.
sources: USDA and university extension postharvest storage guidance
FDA produce storage and safety guidance
entries.kristy_take: Wash it when you eat it, not when you unpack it. Half of what rots in a fridge was rinsed on the way in.
buying_tips: Separate the gas producers (apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes, stone fruit) from greens and berries.
Do not wash anything until you are about to use it.
Never refrigerate: tomatoes, potatoes, onions, garlic, whole melon, unripe stone fruit.
Herbs and asparagus: stand them in a little water, loosely covered.
Greens: dry, with a paper towel in the bag to take up moisture.
Buy at staggered ripeness so the whole week does not turn on Tuesday.
entries.tier_note: Ethylene ripening its neighbors, and moisture rotting a drawer, are both well established.

entries.title: Pasteurized, ultra-pasteurized, homogenized
aliases: why does organic milk last so long
entries.question: What is the difference between pasteurized, ultra-pasteurized and homogenized milk?
entries.decision: Plain pasteurized. Ultra is a shelf-life technology, not better milk.
entries.why: Fewer steps is the whole-food standard. Ultra buys months on a date and costs the milk its character.
entries.short_answer: Fewer steps is the standard here. Pasteurization is a short heat step, around 161F for fifteen seconds. Ultra-pasteurization goes to roughly 280F, which is what puts a date months out on a carton and what makes the milk refuse to culture. Homogenization is not heat at all: it forces the fat into droplets small enough that cream never rises.
entries.detail: These three get muddled constantly. Heat is about shelf life and safety; homogenization is about texture and whether the cream separates. Ultra-pasteurization changes flavor noticeably and makes milk reluctant to culture into yogurt or cheese, which is the practical reason people avoid it rather than a nutritional one. On the whole-food standard the read is simple: fewer processing steps, so plain pasteurized and non-homogenized where the store carries them. That is a preference about processing, not a claim that ultra-pasteurized milk is bad for anyone.
sources: FDA Pasteurized Milk Ordinance (time and temperature standards)
FDA milk labeling and processing definitions
entries.kristy_take: The shortest date on the shelf is usually the least-handled milk.
buying_tips: ‘Ultra-pasteurized’ or ‘UHT’ on the carton explains a date months out.
Ultra-pasteurized milk resists culturing. Skip it for homemade yogurt.
‘Cream-top’ or ‘non-homogenized’ means the fat separates. Shake it.

entries.title: Live cultures, kefir and skyr
entries.question: How do I know the cultures are still alive?
entries.decision: Buy it alive. Heat-treated after culturing is a dead ferment.
entries.why: Heat treatment after culturing ends the ferment. Strained styles hold more protein per spoon.
entries.short_answer: A tub can be yogurt and carry nothing living. What makes one shelf-stable is exactly what ends it, so the cold case is the first filter and the seal is the second. Greek and skyr are strained, which is why they are thicker and carry more protein per spoon. Kefir is a drinkable ferment with a wider mix of cultures than yogurt.
entries.detail: Yogurt is milk plus two required cultures, and everything past that — extra strains, straining, thickeners — is what separates one tub from another. ‘Live and Active Cultures’ is a seal with a defined threshold behind it, and heat-treated shelf-stable yogurts do not carry it, which is the cleanest tell on the shelf. Straining pours off whey and concentrates the protein, which is why a cup of Greek reads so differently from a cup of regular. Kefir ferments with a broader mix of bacteria and yeasts than yogurt does. None of this is a question about sugar; that is the plain-versus-flavored call and it is a separate card.

entries.title: Cream, half-and-half, and ‘creamer’
entries.question: What is the difference between cream and coffee creamer?
entries.decision: Cream or half-and-half. ‘Non-dairy creamer’ is not dairy.
entries.why: Cream has a legal fat minimum. Creamer is oil, sweetener and emulsifiers built to imitate it.
entries.short_answer: Cream is a dairy product with a legal fat minimum: heavy cream is at least 36% milkfat, light whipping 30 to 36, half-and-half 10.5 to 18. ‘Non-dairy creamer’ is not dairy at all. It is typically water or corn syrup solids, an oil, and emulsifiers, flavors and thickeners built to imitate cream. Read the two ingredient lists side by side and it takes three seconds.
entries.detail: Standards of identity fix what cream can mean, which is why those fat percentages are consistent across every carton. Creamer has no such standard because it is a formulated product. The oil in it is usually a refined seed oil, and the sweetness usually comes from corn syrup solids or sugar, with the flavored versions adding more of both. Some cartons of real cream carry stabilizers like carrageenan or gellan gum, so a short list is worth checking on the dairy side too. Whole milk, half-and-half or real cream all do the job with a list you can read out loud.
sources: FDA standards of identity for cream products, 21 CFR 131
FDA food labeling regulations
Product ingredient labeling
entries.kristy_take: Cream is one ingredient. Creamer is a formulation built to look like it. Read the two lists back to back.

entries.title: Flour: bleached, enriched, whole
entries.question: Which flour should I buy, and what does ‘enriched’ mean?
entries.decision: Unbleached all-purpose. Keep whole wheat in the freezer.
entries.why: Protein content picks the flour. Whole wheat keeps the germ, and that oil turns.
entries.short_answer: Protein content picks the flour: bread flour is highest and builds chew, all-purpose is the middle, cake and pastry flour are lowest and stay tender. ‘Enriched’ means B vitamins and iron were added back after refining removed them. ‘Bleached’ means treated with a chemical whitening agent, while ‘unbleached’ was simply aged with air. Whole wheat keeps the bran and germ, so it behaves differently and turns rancid far sooner.
entries.detail: Refining strips the bran and germ and leaves the starchy endosperm, which is what makes white flour pale and shelf-stable. Enrichment is a regulated add-back of thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, folic acid and iron, and it is standard on most white flour sold in the US. Bleaching speeds up the same softening that months of air exposure would have done. Whole wheat still carries the oil in the germ, so it keeps for months rather than years and belongs in the freezer if it is not going quickly. Its bran also cuts gluten strands, which is why an all-whole-wheat loaf comes out denser.
sources: FDA standards of identity for enriched flour, 21 CFR 137
FDA regulations on flour bleaching and maturing agents
USDA FoodData Central

buying_tips: Bread flour for chew, all-purpose for most things, pastry flour for tender.
‘Enriched’ means vitamins and iron added back after refining. Standard on white flour.

entries.tier_note: Bleached, enriched and whole are defined terms, and the germ’s oil turning is simply what fat does.

entries.title: Buying from the bulk bins
entries.question: Is the bulk bin section actually a good deal?
entries.decision: Bulk for dry staples. Careful with anything oily.
entries.why: Turnover is everything. Oil goes rancid in a slow bin, whatever the price says.
entries.short_answer: For anything with fast turnover, yes. Grains, beans, lentils, oats, rice and especially spices are dramatically cheaper by weight, and you buy exactly what you need. The catch is turnover: nuts, seeds and whole-grain flours carry oil that goes rancid, so a slow bin is a bad buy at any price. Look at whether the bin is full and busy, and smell what you scoop.
entries.detail: Bulk pricing strips out the packaging and the brand, which is most of what a shelf-stable staple costs. Spices are the extreme case, where a scoop from a bin costs a fraction of the same weight in a jar and is usually fresher because the bin moves. The risk sits entirely with the fatty items. Rancidity is the real quality question in this aisle, and it announces itself: rancid nuts and seeds smell like old paint or crayons and taste sharp and bitter. Bring your own jars where the store allows it, and note the tare weight.
sources: FDA retail bulk food handling guidance
USDA FoodData Central
entries.kristy_take: Bulk is unbeatable on grains, beans and spices. On nuts and whole-grain flour it depends entirely on how fast that bin moves.
buying_tips: Best value: rice, oats, beans, lentils, dried fruit and especially spices.
Riskiest: nuts, seeds and whole-grain flours. Oil goes rancid in a slow bin.
Full busy bins turn over. A dusty half-empty one does not.
Smell it before it goes in the cart. Rancid reads as paint, crayon or bitter.
Buy what you will use in a month, and store it airtight and dark.
entries.tier_note: Rancidity in a slow bin is real. Which bins to trust is a shopping standard, not a rule.

entries.title: Telling when fats have turned
aliases: how to tell if oil is rancid
entries.question: How do I tell if nuts, oil or flour have gone rancid?
entries.decision: Smell it. Old paint or crayons means it is spent.
entries.why: Rancid fat tastes sharp and bitter, with a scratch that does not fade. Quality, not safety.
entries.short_answer: Smell and taste, and trust them. Rancid fat smells like old paint, crayons, putty or nail polish, and it tastes sharp and bitter with a scratch at the back of the throat that does not fade. It happens to nuts, seeds, whole-grain flour, wheat germ, nut butters and every oil. It is a quality problem rather than a safety emergency: the food is spent, and it will make whatever you put it in taste bad.
entries.detail: Oxidation is fat reacting with air, and light, heat and time all speed it up. That is the whole reason good olive oil comes in dark glass and gets stored away from the stove, and why whole-grain flour keeps months while white flour keeps almost indefinitely. The peppery catch at the back of the throat in fresh olive oil is a different sensation from the flat bitter scratch of a rancid one, and the difference is learnable in a single side-by-side taste. Once you can smell it, the bulk bin, the back of the pantry and the half-used oil bottle all become easy calls.
sources: Peer-reviewed literature on lipid oxidation in foods
UC Davis Olive Center sensory standards for olive oil defects
entries.kristy_take: Old paint and crayons is the smell. Once you know it, half the back of the pantry starts making sense.
buying_tips: Smell nuts and seeds before they go in the cart, especially from a bulk bin.
Rancid reads as paint, crayon, putty or nail polish. Sharp and bitter on the tongue.
Dark glass or tin for oil, stored away from the stove rather than beside it.
Nuts, seeds, whole-grain flour and nut butters keep far longer in the fridge or freezer.
Buy oil in a size you will finish in a couple of months rather than the big bottle.
entries.tier_note: Rancid fat is a quality problem rather than a safety one, and it is flagged on exactly that basis.

entries.title: Buying real extra-virgin olive oil
entries.question: How do I buy real extra-virgin olive oil, and what do the grades mean?
entries.decision: Extra virgin, a recent harvest date, one country.
entries.why: Olive oil is widely adulterated. ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ all mean refined oil.
entries.short_answer: Extra virgin is mechanically extracted with no heat or solvent and has to pass both a chemical limit and a taste panel. Virgin is the same process with a looser limit. ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ all mean refined oil blended with a little virgin back in, and ‘light’ refers to color and taste rather than calories. Past the grade, olive oil is one of the more adulterated products in the store, so the three signals that matter are a recent harvest date, a dark bottle, and a single country of origin.
entries.detail: Grade and provenance are two separate checks and a bottle has to pass both. On grade: pomace oil is solvent-extracted from the paste left after pressing and is a different product; ‘first cold pressed’ is a legacy phrase with no added legal force. On provenance: ‘packed in [country]’ names where it was bottled, not where the olives grew, and ‘product of’ is the phrase that names the origin. A harvest date beats a best-by date every time, because the oil degrades from the day it is pressed. Dark glass or tin protects it from light, and a price that is unusually low for extra-virgin is a flag rather than a find.
sources: International Olive Council trade standard for olive oils
USDA AMS United States Standards for Grades of Olive Oil (voluntary)
FDA labeling rules on country of origin
entries.kristy_take: Harvest date, dark bottle, one country. Everything else on the front is decoration.

Look for a HARVEST date, not just ‘best by’ — and buy recent.

Single country of origin, named with ‘product of’.

entries.title: Reading a nut butter jar
entries.question: What should be in a jar of peanut butter?
entries.decision: Peanuts and salt. No-stir means an oil was added.
entries.why: No-stir texture comes from added palm or hydrogenated oil, and usually sugar with it.
entries.short_answer: Peanuts. Salt if you want it. That is the whole list on the good jars. The no-stir versions get their texture from added palm oil or hydrogenated oil, and most also add sugar. Oil sitting on top is not a fault, it is the sign that nothing was added to stop it. Stir it in once, then keep the jar upside down in the fridge.
entries.detail: The separation people complain about is what natural peanut butter does, because ground peanuts are peanuts and oil. Stabilizers fix the texture and turn it into a product with a longer ingredient list. Sugar shows up in most conventional jars, and reduced-fat versions typically replace the removed fat with sugar and starch, which is the opposite of the trade most people think they are making. The same reading applies to almond, cashew and sunflower butters. One or two ingredients on the back is the standard, and it is easy to find.
sources: FDA standards of identity for peanut butter, 21 CFR 164.150
Product ingredient labeling
USDA FoodData Central
entries.kristy_take: Peanuts, and maybe salt. Oil on top means nothing was added to stop it, which is the point.
buying_tips: The list should read peanuts, and salt if you want it. Nothing else is needed.
Oil separated on top is the good sign — nothing was added to hold it in.

entries.title: Grains beyond rice
entries.question: What else should I be buying besides rice?
entries.decision: Rotate them, and cook them like pasta in salted water.
entries.why: Bulgur, quinoa and buckwheat are fast. Farro and barley are made for soups and bowls.
entries.short_answer: Rotating grains is the cheapest upgrade in the pantry. Quinoa cooks in fifteen minutes and holds together cold. Farro and barley are chewy and made for soups and grain bowls. Buckwheat is not wheat at all and cooks fast. Millet and sorghum are cheap and carry no gluten. Bulgur is the fastest of the lot: ten minutes with boiling water and a lid.
entries.detail: Variety is worth it on its own terms, since different grains bring different textures and cooking times, and rotating them means no single crop is the base of every meal. That matters practically as well, because rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and water than other grains, so it is the one not to build every dinner on. Most of these cook like pasta, in plenty of salted water and drained when tender, which is far more forgiving than the exact ratios rice wants. Buy them from the bulk bins where you can.
sources: USDA FoodData Central
FDA guidance on inorganic arsenic in rice
Whole Grains Council grain reference
entries.kristy_take: Cook them like pasta: lots of salted water, drain when tender. Far easier than getting a rice ratio right.
buying_tips: Quick: bulgur (10 min), quinoa (15 min), buckwheat (15 min), millet (20 min).
Chewy and slow: farro, barley, wheat berries, sorghum. Made for soups and bowls.
Buckwheat, millet, sorghum and quinoa carry no gluten. Barley, farro and bulgur do.

entries.title: Front vs. back
aliases: how to read a food label
entries.question: Where on a package should I actually be looking?
entries.decision: Turn it over. Decide from the back.
entries.why: The front is written by marketing. The back is written by law.
entries.short_answer: The front of a package is advertising and the back is regulated. Every phrase on the front (natural, wholesome, farm fresh, made with real, lightly sweetened) is chosen by a marketing team, and only some of them have any legal definition at all. The ingredient list and the Nutrition Facts panel have to be true and have to follow a format. Turn it over first, and the front becomes noise.
entries.detail: This is the one habit that makes every other label question easy. Nearly all of the confusion in a grocery store comes from front-of-pack language, which is written to imply more than it commits to, and almost none of it comes from the panel on the back, which is defined down to the font. Three things on the back do most of the work: the ingredient list in descending order by weight, the added-sugars line, and the serving size the numbers are based on. When the front and the back disagree, the back is the one that had to be checked.
sources: FDA food labeling regulations, 21 CFR Part 101
FTC guidance on food advertising claims
entries.kristy_take: The front is written by marketing. The back is written by law. Turn it over.
buying_tips: Turn it over first. Decide from the back, then look at the front if at all.
Ingredient list, added-sugars line, serving size. Those three answer most questions.
Front-of-pack words like natural, wholesome and farm fresh carry little or no definition.

entries.tier_note: The panel’s contents are mandated and the front of the box is not. That asymmetry is the whole rule.

entries.title: Ingredients are in weight order
entries.question: How do I read an ingredient list properly?
entries.decision: Read the first three ingredients, then the added-sugar line.
entries.why: The list runs in weight order. Split sugars keep any one of them from climbing it.
entries.short_answer: Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so the first three tell you most of what is in the package. Everything after ‘contains 2% or less of’ can appear in any order and is a trace amount. The trick worth knowing is sugar splitting: a product can list cane syrup, dextrose, juice concentrate and honey separately so no single one climbs the list, when together they would sit near the top.
entries.detail: The weight-order rule is the most useful thing on any package, because it turns a list into a ranking. A bread whose first ingredient is ‘whole wheat flour’ is a different food from one whose first ingredient is ‘enriched wheat flour’, whatever the bag says. The 2%-or-less clause exists because ordering trace additives serves nobody, and it also means everything below that line is a rounding error. Sugar splitting is legal and common, and the added-sugars line on the Nutrition Facts panel is the counter to it, because it totals them all whatever they were called.
sources: FDA ingredient labeling requirements, 21 CFR 101.4
FDA Nutrition Facts label final rule (added sugars declaration)
entries.kristy_take: First three ingredients, then the added-sugar line. That is a whole label read in ten seconds.
buying_tips: Read the first three. They are most of the package by weight.
Everything after ‘contains 2% or less of’ is a trace amount, in any order.
Watch for split sugars: syrups, concentrates, dextrose and honey listed separately.
The added-sugars line totals them all, whatever each one was named.
A first ingredient of ‘enriched wheat flour’ is not ‘whole wheat flour’.

labels_decoded.meaning: The required order of the main ingredient list.
Everything after this point is a trace amount, and not in weight order.

watch_out: Everything after “contains 2% or less of” is a trace, and not in weight order.

entries.title: Judging any seal on any package
entries.question: How do I know if a seal on a package means anything?
entries.decision: A published standard and an outside auditor, or it is a sticker.
entries.why: A badge a company gave itself has neither. Each real seal covers one scope.
entries.short_answer: Ask three questions of any seal. Who set the standard, is it published, and does an independent body audit against it. A badge a company created for its own products answers none of the three. USDA Organic, Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, Global Animal Partnership, American Grassfed and the Non-GMO Project all publish standards and use outside auditors. What no seal tells you is anything it never set out to measure.
entries.detail: The gap between a certification and a marketing badge is entirely in the audit. Real programs publish their standard, so anyone can read exactly what was checked, and they send inspectors. The second half of reading a seal is scope: an organic seal covers inputs and practices and says nothing about welfare beyond a baseline, a welfare seal says nothing about pesticides, and a non-GMO seal addresses one issue only. Stacking seals on a package does not make it a better food, it makes it a food that paid for several audits. The ingredient panel still decides what the thing actually is.
sources: USDA National Organic Program certification requirements
Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved and Global Animal Partnership published standards
Non-GMO Project verification standard
American Grassfed Association standards
entries.kristy_take: A badge a company gave itself is a sticker. The real ones publish, and they inspect.
buying_tips: Look for a named program, not a decorative badge. If the standard cannot be looked up, it is marketing.
Each seal covers one scope. Organic is not welfare, welfare is not pesticides, non-GMO is neither.
Third-party audited beats self-declared, every time.

entries.title: ‘Cold-pressed’, ‘expeller-pressed’, ‘refined’
entries.question: What do ‘cold-pressed’ and ‘expeller-pressed’ mean on an oil?
entries.decision: Pressed, not extracted. ‘Refined’ is the word that gives it away.
entries.why: Expeller and cold-pressed are both mechanical. Most supermarket oil is neither.
entries.short_answer: Two of these words describe pressing and one describes what happens afterwards. Expeller-pressed means a mechanical screw press with no solvent, though friction still generates heat. Cold-pressed is the same press with the temperature held down, and for olive oil in the EU that is a defined limit. Most supermarket cooking oil is neither: it is solvent-extracted, then refined, bleached and deodorized.
entries.detail: Extraction and refining are two separate steps and both matter. Mechanical pressing leaves more of the original flavor, color and aroma in the oil, which is exactly why unrefined oils taste like the thing they came from and refined ones taste like nothing. Solvent extraction pulls far more oil out of the same seed, which is why it dominates at commercial scale and why those oils are cheap. In the US ‘cold-pressed’ has no federal definition for most oils, so it carries less weight on a sunflower bottle than on an olive one. Processing is the honest basis for preferring the pressed version, and that is a whole-food-standard call rather than a settled finding.
sources: International Olive Council definitions of cold extraction
FDA labeling regulations (no federal definition of ‘cold-pressed’ for most oils)
Food-science references on solvent extraction and oil refining

entries.title: ‘Sugar-free’ and what replaced the sugar
entries.question: If it says sugar-free, what is doing the sweetening?
entries.decision: Read what replaced the sugar. ‘Unsweetened’ is the plainer word.
entries.why: ‘Sugar-free’ is a defined claim about what came out. The list names what went in.
entries.short_answer: Something else, and the ingredient list names it. ‘Sugar-free’ is a defined claim, under half a gram of sugar per serving, so the sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol (erythritol, maltitol, xylitol) or a high-intensity sweetener (stevia, monk fruit, sucralose, aspartame). ‘Unsweetened’ is the plainer word and generally means nothing sweet was added at all. The two are not interchangeable.
entries.detail: ‘Sugar-free’ answers a Nutrition Facts question and says nothing about what took sugar’s place, which is why the ingredient list matters more here than on almost any other claim. Sugar alcohols appear by name and are also totalled on the panel; high-intensity sweeteners appear in the list and are used in tiny amounts. ‘Unsweetened’ has no formal FDA definition and in practice means no sweetener of any kind, including the non-caloric ones, which makes it the cleaner word to look for on yogurt, plant milk and apple sauce. ‘Naturally sweetened’ has no definition at all and covers honey, maple syrup and juice concentrate.
sources: FDA nutrient content claims for sugars, 21 CFR 101.60
FDA guidance on high-intensity sweeteners
FDA Nutrition Facts label final rule (sugar alcohol declaration)
entries.kristy_take: ‘Sugar-free’ tells you what came out. The ingredient list tells you what went in instead. Read that one.

entries.title: Seafood labels: wild, farm-raised, origin
entries.question: What has to be on a seafood label?
entries.decision: Species, method, country. All three required, and none stops substitution.
entries.why: All three are required on unprocessed seafood. Origin can mean where it was processed.
entries.short_answer: Three things are required on most unprocessed fish and shellfish at retail: the species name, whether it was wild-caught or farm-raised, and the country of origin. That is federal country-of-origin labeling, and it is one of the few places a store must tell you where food came from. The catch is that origin can mean where it was processed rather than where it was caught.
entries.detail: Country-of-origin labeling covers unprocessed fish and shellfish and is genuinely useful, since it turns ‘farm-raised, product of ___‘ into a readable pair rather than a guess. Two limits are worth knowing. Cooked, breaded or otherwise processed seafood falls outside the rule. And species naming has a long history of substitution, where a cheaper fish is sold under a pricier name, which is a far bigger problem on a bare fillet than on a whole fish or a piece with the skin left on. Buying whole, buying skin-on, and buying from a counter that can answer the origin question are the practical defenses.

FDA Seafood List (acceptable market names)
Peer-reviewed and government studies of seafood species substitution

entries.title: Serving size and the numbers under it
entries.question: Why do the numbers on the panel look so low?
entries.decision: Read the top two lines before any of the numbers.
entries.why: Every number is per serving. Half of what looks reasonable is a third of the package.
entries.short_answer: Because every number on the Nutrition Facts panel is per serving, and the servings-per-container line above it says how many of those the package holds. ‘About 2.5 servings’ means multiplying everything by two and a half. Serving sizes are set by regulation to reflect what people typically eat, not what is good for anyone, and larger single-serve packages now have to show a per-package column too.
entries.detail: This is the easiest number on a package to misread, and it is not an accident that it sits at the top in small type. The reference amounts are fixed by the FDA per food category, so competing products in the same category are genuinely comparable, which is the useful thing about them. What they are not is a recommendation. The 2016 label rules made serving sizes more realistic, put added sugars on their own line, and required dual-column labelling on packages that could plausibly be finished in one sitting. Read from the top down: servings per container first, serving size second, then the numbers.

FDA Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed, 21 CFR 101.12

entries.title: Raw kefir
entries.question: Is raw kefir worth buying?
entries.decision: The best thing a farm does with its milk. Buy it cultured.
entries.why: A live ferment from a named herd. The refrigerated case is the only place it exists.
entries.card_why: Kefir is what a dairy does with milk it wants to keep, and it has been doing it for centuries. The grains turn it tangy and thick and it holds for weeks where the milk holds for days. The rule is the milk’s rule: the farm is the product. Buy it from the herd you would drink from raw, as close to the culture date as the case allows.
entries.short_answer: Raw kefir is a live ferment and it has to be sold cold. Anything shelf-stable was heat-treated after culturing, which ends the thing you were buying it for.
entries.detail: Kefir carries a wider mix of cultures than yogurt and pours rather than spoons. Made from raw milk it is the same sourcing question as the milk: a named farm, a small herd, a cold chain. Plain is the only version worth buying — the flavored tubs carry the added sugar of a dessert and the ferment becomes the excuse.
entries.kristy_take: Same farm as the milk, or it is just a drink.
buying_tips: The same farm name as the milk. Kefir is only as good as what went into it.
A culture or bottling date on the bottle, not only a best-by.
Glass, and a pour thick enough to cling to the side.
Plain. Sweetened kefir is a dessert wearing a ferment’s name.

entries.title: Raw aged cheese
entries.question: Is raw milk cheese worth buying?
entries.decision: Start here. The one raw dairy sitting in plain sight.
entries.why: US law allows raw cheese at sixty days, so the good counter already stocks it.
entries.card_why: Aged raw-milk cheese is the raw dairy nobody has to hunt for — US rules allow it at sixty days and up, so a decent cheese counter already keeps a case of it. Sixty days of aging is a technology of its own, and it is the reason an aged raw cheddar tastes of the place it came from while a young commodity block tastes of very little. The organizing principle is the milk’s: ask who made it, from which herd, and how long it sat.
entries.short_answer: Look for “raw milk” or “lait cru” on the rind label with an age beside it, and buy from the cut-to-order counter rather than the pre-wrapped wall.
entries.detail: The sixty-day rule is why raw cheese is legal at US retail where raw milk often is not. Aging concentrates the cheese and develops it, and a raw-milk cheese carries the character of one herd and one season in a way a standardized pasteurized curd is designed not to. A staffed counter can usually name the maker, the animal and the age, which is exactly the information the rind label is too small to hold.
entries.kristy_take: Ask the monger who made it. A good one has been waiting to tell you.
buying_tips: “Raw milk” or “lait cru” printed on the rind label, with an age beside it.
A named maker and a named herd, not just a country of origin.
The cut-to-order counter over the pre-wrapped wall.
Hard, aged styles first — alpine, aged cheddar, manchego, pecorino.
Keep the rinds. They belong in a pot of beans or soup.
watch_out: “Pasteurized process cheese”, “cheese product” and “cheese food” are progressively less cheese.
Raw dairy is not for every household. The raw milk card names who, once.

labels_decoded.meaning: Made from unpasteurized milk. At US retail it also means aged 60 days or more.
Heated below pasteurization. Not raw, and not fully pasteurized either.

entries.title: Sprouts
entries.question: Are sprouts worth buying?
entries.decision: Buy them cold and crisp, or grow them on the counter.
entries.why: A living food sold warm is the only real problem. Cold case or your own jar.
entries.card_why: Sprouts are about as alive as produce gets — a seed caught mid-decision, sold days old. That is the appeal and it is also the whole handling question, because the warm damp days that sprout a seed are the same days that sprout everything else. A grower who keeps them cold from the sprouting room to the case is doing the only thing that matters. Past that, a jar and a screen on your own counter costs almost nothing and puts the sourcing question entirely in your hands.
entries.short_answer: Cold case, roots still white, no sour smell in the clamshell. Anything sitting at room temperature has been given the conditions it was grown in.
entries.detail: Sprouting has been a winter green in kitchens for a very long time, and a jar with a mesh lid on the counter still produces a crop in three or four days for the price of a scoop of seed. Broccoli, alfalfa, radish and mung are the usual four. Buying them instead is fine when the case is cold and the turnover is quick; the clamshell tells you plainly when it is not, because sprouts go slick and sour before they look wrong.
entries.kristy_take: Grow them yourself and the sourcing question answers itself.
buying_tips: The refrigerated case only. Room-temperature sprouts have been left in growing conditions.
Roots still white and threadlike, stems crisp rather than limp.
No condensation fogging the clamshell and no sour smell through the vents.
A pack date you can read. Days old, not a week.
Or a jar, a mesh lid and a scoop of seed. Three days on the counter.
watch_out: Not for pregnancy or anyone immunocompromised. Growers and the FDA agree on this one.
Slick, browning or sour-smelling sprouts are past it. That happens fast and it is visible.

labels_decoded.meaning: Germinated seed, eaten whole with the root. Sold within days.
Grown in medium and cut above the root. A different product, handled like a leafy green.
